I started writing this at 3:17 a.m. because the apartment was finally quiet. The radiator had stopped ticking. The neighbor’s dog had given up. The street below, which is usually a thin river of headlights and delivery scooters, was empty except for a single taxi idling at the corner and turning its sign off. It is the hour when the city holds its breath, and I like to think that if you listen hard enough you can hear it think.

There is a particular kind of freedom that comes with writing at this hour. No one expects anything. No emails are due. No one is going to read it yet, or maybe never. You are not writing for an audience, you are writing for the version of yourself that will exist tomorrow morning and will wake up with a headache and wonder what you were doing. That version will read the sentences and try to understand the logic. It will probably fail.

I have lived in this building for seven years. The building is not special. It is a pre-war walk-up with a laundry room that smells of mildew and a super who only comes on Tuesdays. On the third floor, Mrs. Kowalski keeps a ficus that has survived three moves and one divorce. On the fifth floor, a kid practices violin badly from four to five every day. I have heard every variation of that piece until I know the squeaks. I have come to love the squeaks.

The first time I noticed the time, really noticed it, was when I was twenty-two and working nights at a 24-hour copy shop on 8th Avenue. The shop had a glass front and fluorescent lights that hummed in B flat. People would come in at 2 a.m. with boxes of things they needed duplicated before a morning deadline. Grad students with theses. Lawyers with briefs. Once a man came in with a wedding invitation and asked us to make 300 copies. It was 3 a.m. on a Saturday. He said his fiancée had forgotten to order them. We did it. He cried a little.

That job taught me that the night is not empty. It is just a different kind of crowded. The people who are out then are either escaping something or looking for something, and often it is the same thing. At 3 a.m., the world is honest. The masks come off because there is no one to perform for. You can buy a bottle of water in pajamas. You can cry on the subway and no one will film it.

I think about time a lot, maybe too much. We treat it like a straight line, but it isn’t. It folds. It stacks. It loops. I can be making coffee at 7 a.m. and suddenly I am twenty-six again, standing in that copy shop, watching the copier jam on page 147 of someone’s dissertation on medieval beekeeping. I can be walking my dog and be eight years old, watching ants carry crumbs up a sidewalk crack. Memory is not a file cabinet. It is a city you walk through. Some streets are well lit. Some are dark and you have to feel your way.

Last winter I lost a notebook. A small black one with a soft cover, the kind that doesn’t scream. I had been carrying it for months. I wrote grocery lists in it, bad ideas, overheard conversations, the names of birds I couldn’t identify. I wrote a letter to my father I never sent. I wrote the first paragraph of a novel three times and erased it each time. I left it on the Q train. I realized it when I got to work and the pocket was empty. I got back on the train at the next stop and rode it backwards for four stops, asking people if they’d seen it. No one had. The train was full of people who had their own notebooks, their own empty pockets.

I never found it. Sometimes I think someone is reading it right now. Maybe they are using it for grocery lists. Maybe they are reading the unsent letter and wondering who I am. The thought is comforting, in a strange way. The idea that my private words could be in circulation, being misread, being useful for someone else’s eggs and milk. It means the work is not wasted. It means it has left me.

Writing, for me, is not a vocation. It is a habit like brushing teeth, except I do it poorly and often at the wrong time. I write when I am anxious. I write when I am bored. I write when I am happy because I am afraid the feeling will leave and I want proof it existed. The proof is never proof enough. The words are always thinner than the feeling.

There is a café on my block that opens at six. The owner, Luis, knows my order. He doesn’t ask. He just puts it down. In the morning he is quiet, tired. At night, when he closes, he sits on a milk crate out back and smokes. I have seen him there through the window, staring at nothing. I wonder what he thinks about. Probably not about literature. Probably about rent, his daughter, the broken espresso machine. That’s good. That’s real.

We want our lives to be stories with arcs. We want the night shift to mean something. We want the lost notebook to be a metaphor. But most of it is just accumulation. The radiator ticks. The dog barks. The violin squeaks. The taxi turns its sign off. You keep going.

I used to believe that if I wrote enough, I would understand myself. Now I think I write because I don’t understand myself, and the act of writing is a way to keep the not-understanding company. It’s like leaving a light on for a guest who may never arrive. You don’t know why you do it. You just know the room feels wrong when it’s dark.

My mother calls every Sunday. She asks if I am eating. I say yes. She asks if I am writing. I say yes. She doesn’t ask what. She knows better. She knows that telling you what you are writing is like opening a present too early. It loses the shape.

Sometimes I think about the people who never get to write. The night shift nurses, the Uber drivers, the people who clean offices after hours. They are writing all the time, in their heads. They have whole novels in there. They have the unsent letters, the arguments, the dreams. They just don’t have the time or the energy or the permission to put it down. I think about that and feel guilty for having a notebook, even a lost one.

The city at 3 a.m. is not romantic. It smells like exhaust and wet concrete. The streetlights make pools of yellow that don’t reach the cracks. Pigeons sleep on ledges. A sanitation truck rolls by, slow and hydraulic. It is beautiful in the way that anything honest is beautiful: not pretty, but true.

I am writing this now and I have no idea where it is going. That is the best part. When you know where you are going, you are just transcribing. When you don’t know, you are listening. You are letting the city think through you.

I think about the word “freely.” It sounds simple. Write freely. As if freedom is a state you can enter like a room. But freedom is not a room. It is the moment you stop worrying about the lock. It is the moment you realize the door was never locked.

So I will keep writing. Not because it will be good. Not because it will be read. Because the radiator is quiet, the street is empty, and the taxi has left. Because there is a ficus on the third floor and a violin on the fifth. Because somewhere a notebook is being used for grocery lists. Because the night is honest.

I will write until the sun comes up and the building wakes up and Mrs. Kowalski waters her plant and Luis opens the café and the kid starts practicing again. I will write until the words stop feeling like mine and start feeling like the city’s. I will write until I am tired enough to sleep and then I will dream in sentences.

If you are reading this, thank you. If you are not, thank you too. It doesn’t matter. The writing happened. The hour passed. The taxi turned its sign off and drove away. The city exhaled.

I should stop soon. The light is getting thin at the edge of the blinds. It is almost 4 a.m. The world is about to start again, with all its noise and its demands and its beautiful, ordinary mess. I will be here. I will be writing.
